I leaned back in my leather executive chair, rubbing the bridge of my nose as a tired smile tugged at the corner of my lips. "My name is Julian, Clara. You've been running this entire household for two weeks now; I think you've earned the right to drop the formal title when we're off the clock."

Clara hesitated, her cheeks flushing a faint, delicate pink under the warm lamplight. "It feels a bit strange calling my boss by his first name."

"Try it," I challenged gently, tilting my head. "Just once."

She took a breath, her dark eyes meeting mine with a quiet, lingering intensity. "Julian."

The way she said my name—without hesitation, without hidden agendas, without the sycophantic reverence everyone else in my circle used—sent a strange, electric warmth straight through my chest. It wasn't the artificial adoration Vanessa had feigned; it was something grounded, real, and profoundly comforting.

"Thank you," I said, gesturing to the tea and scones. "And thank you for this. You're spoiling me."

"Consider it hazard pay for dealing with your stubbornness," she replied with a dry, playful wit I hadn't seen before. She stepped toward the door, then paused, looking back at the stacks of legal paperwork covering my desk. "The trial starts next month, doesn't it?"

My expression darkened slightly. "Yes. Federal court. Martin and Daniel are trying to cut a plea deal, blaming each other for tampering with the car brakes. But the forensic evidence is airtight. They'll be spending a very long time behind bars."

Clara walked slowly back toward the desk, her expression turning serious. "Does it still hurt? Knowing family could do that to you?"

I looked down at my hands, resting flat on the mahogany surface. For years, I had believed that strength meant never showing vulnerability, that maintaining the Sterling empire required an unyielding, emotional armor. The accident had cracked that armor, and the betrayal had shattered it entirely.

"It doesn't hurt anymore," I confessed quietly, looking back up into her eyes. "It just... clarified things. For a long time, I thought wealth and power were shields against loneliness. But sitting in that wheelchair at the ballroom, surrounded by hundreds of people drinking my champagne while I was supposedly paralyzed... I realized I was completely alone. Nobody cared about me. They only cared about what I could do for them."

"Not everyone," Clara whispered, her voice barely audible over the hum of the desk lamp.

I froze. The space between us suddenly felt charged with an electricity that had nothing to do with corporate power or legal battles. I stood up from my chair, moving slowly around the desk until I was standing right in front of her.

She didn't step back. Her gaze remained locked on mine, steady and unafraid.

"No," I murmured, reaching out to gently tuck a stray strand of dark hair behind her ear. Her skin was warm, and she let out a soft, involuntary breath at the touch. "Not everyone."

For a long moment, the world outside the study—the federal trials, the media storms, the multi-billion-dollar corporation—simply vanished. There was only the quiet tick of the grandfather clock in the hallway, the scent of cinnamon and tea, and the undeniable pull drawing us together.
